title: Beneficiary Designation Audit
learning_objectives: Understand that beneficiary designations trump wills
Identify common beneficiary designation mistakes and their consequences
Create proper beneficiary designation strategy for different life stages
description: Interactive audit tool analyzing four case studies of beneficiary mistakes, followed by practice creating proper designations for various life situations, and personal beneficiary audit checklist creation.
instructions: Analyze four real-world beneficiary mistakes and their consequences
Calculate financial and family impact of each mistake
Practice proper beneficiary planning for sample situations
Identify life events triggering beneficiary reviews

what_are_beneficiary_designations.definition: Forms used to name who receives specific accounts/assets directly upon your death, bypassing your will and probate
what_are_beneficiary_designations.key_principle: Beneficiary designations TRUMP wills—they control distribution regardless of what your will says
accounts_with_beneficiaries: Individual Retirement Accounts (Traditional IRA, Roth IRA, SEP-IRA, SIMPLE IRA)

primary_vs_contingent.primary_beneficiary: First in line—receives assets if alive at your death
primary_vs_contingent.contingent_beneficiary: Backup—receives assets only if primary beneficiary has died before you
primary_vs_contingent.critical_rule: ALWAYS name contingent beneficiaries. Without them, assets go to your estate (probate) if primary predeceases you.

why_beneficiaries_matter.probate_avoidance: Properly designated accounts transfer immediately without court involvement
why_beneficiaries_matter.speed: Beneficiaries typically receive assets within weeks, not months/years
why_beneficiaries_matter.often_largest_assets: For many people, retirement accounts and life insurance represent majority of wealth—these pass by beneficiary, not will

case_studies.title: The Forgotten Ex-Spouse

situation.marital_history: Divorced from Lisa 8 years ago; remarried to Rachel 5 years ago

legal_battle.argument: Michael intended to provide for current wife, obviously didn't mean to leave majority to ex
legal_battle.court_ruling: Beneficiary designations control regardless of intent. Lisa receives $580K.

outcome.family_impact: Rachel financially devastated; Lisa received windfall she didn't expect or need; Michael's wishes completely thwarted; family relationships destroyed

case_studies.lesson: Update beneficiaries IMMEDIATELY after divorce. Many states automatically revoke ex-spouses, but don't rely on this—update explicitly.
case_studies.cost_of_mistake: $580,000 went to wrong person; $45,000 in litigation; 18 months of family warfare
case_studies.prevention: Update beneficiaries within 30 days of divorce finalization. Make it part of divorce checklist.

case_studies.title: Minor Children Named Directly

situation.intent: Wanted to ensure daughter received everything

court_action.custodianship: Court appointed Amanda's sister as custodian under UTMA (Uniform Transfer to Minors Act)
court_action.restrictions: Sister could only use funds for Sophia's 'benefit' until age 18
court_action.oversight: Required annual court accountings and approval for major expenses
court_action.cost: $3,000 in legal fees to establish custodianship

age_18_outcome.what_happened: Sophia received $325,000 lump sum at age 18 (original $325K + 10 years growth)
age_18_outcome.result: 18-year-old with no financial experience received $325,000 all at once
consequences: Loaned money to friends ($40,000 never repaid)
No college degree, no remaining money

case_studies.lesson: NEVER name minor children as direct beneficiaries. Instead, name a trust as beneficiary with terms controlling distribution (e.g., 1/3 at 25, 1/3 at 30, 1/3 at 35).

better_approach.solution: Create testamentary trust in will OR revocable living trust
better_approach.trustee_manages: Responsible adult manages funds for child's benefit
better_approach.controlled_distribution: Release portions at maturity milestones (25, 30, 35) or for specific purposes (education, health, home purchase)

case_studies.cost_of_mistake: $325,000 wasted; daughter's education compromised; intent completely defeated

case_studies.title: My Estate as Beneficiary

situation.family: Married to Susan, two adult children

beneficiaries.ira: My Estate - Robert thought this would follow his will
beneficiaries.will: Everything split: 50% to wife, 25% each to children

outcome.problem: Naming 'estate' defeats the entire purpose of beneficiary designations

consequences.public_record: All assets, beneficiaries, and amounts became public record

tax_inefficiency.ira_problem: Estate as beneficiary loses 'inherited IRA' tax advantages
tax_inefficiency.must_distribute: IRA must be distributed within 5 years (instead of stretching over beneficiaries' lifetimes)
tax_inefficiency.tax_acceleration: Forced Susan and children into higher tax brackets
tax_inefficiency.additional_taxes: $135,000 in additional income taxes versus inherited IRA

case_studies.lesson: NEVER name 'my estate' as beneficiary unless you specifically want probate. Name individuals or trust directly.

correct_approach.life_insurance: Primary: Trust for children; Contingent: Children directly
correct_approach.result: No probate, inherited IRA tax benefits preserved, immediate distribution

case_studies.cost_of_mistake: $185,500 in probate costs and unnecessary taxes + 14-month delay

case_studies.title: No Contingent Beneficiaries

situation.family: Widow (husband died 3 years earlier), two adult children
situation.problem: Mother died 6 months before Karen (at age 89)

outcome.what_happened: With no contingent beneficiaries and primary deceased, accounts defaulted to estate

consequences.distribution: Eventually to children per will, but after probate delay and cost

outcome.preventable_cost: $23,500 + 11-month delay—easily prevented by naming contingent beneficiaries

case_studies.lesson: ALWAYS name contingent beneficiaries for every account. Review and update if contingents die.

correct_approach.always_have_backup: Primary: Mother; Contingent: Two children equally
correct_approach.review_annually: When mother died, Karen should have updated primary to children and named new contingents
correct_approach.result_if_correct: Direct transfer to children, no probate, no delay

case_studies.cost_of_mistake: $23,500 + 11-month delay—simply for neglecting to name contingents

scenario_a.situation: Single, Age 25, $15K in 401(k), Dating but Not Engaged

recommendation.rationale: Simple situation, no dependents, standard succession. DON'T name girlfriend/boyfriend unless engaged—relationships change.

scenario_a.when_to_update: When engaged/married, name partner. Until then, family is appropriate.

scenario_b.situation: Married, Ages 30/32, Two Young Children, $200K Combined Retirement, $250K Life Insurance Each

retirement_accounts.primary: Spouse (tax benefits for spousal inherited IRA)
retirement_accounts.rationale: Spouse-to-spouse transfer preserves tax advantages. If both die, trust protects children from lump sum at 18.

life_insurance.rationale: Each spouse has own insurance. If both die, life insurance funds children's trust. Spouse doesn't need their own life insurance as beneficiary.

scenario_b.critical_action: Create testamentary trust in will OR revocable living trust to serve as beneficiary for children

scenario_c.situation: Recently Divorced Parent, Age 37, One Child (Age 10), $180K Retirement, $500K Life Insurance
scenario_c.current_status: All beneficiaries still list ex-spouse from marriage

recommendation.immediate_action: URGENT—Change ALL beneficiaries from ex-spouse immediately

retirement_accounts.contingent: Child's guardian or sibling (as backup trustee)
retirement_accounts.rationale: Child age 10 cannot receive directly. Trust ensures management.

life_insurance.rationale: Ensure child's financial security with professional management

scenario_c.urgency: CRITICAL—this is the #1 priority after divorce. If died tomorrow, ex-spouse gets everything.

scenario_d.situation: Engaged Couple, Ages 27/28, Planning Marriage in 6 Months, Each Has $50K in Various Accounts

recommendation.before_marriage: Keep parents as beneficiaries until legally married

after_marriage.rationale: Once married, spouse should be primary. Don't name each other before marriage unless you want parents excluded entirely.

scenario_d.timeline: Update immediately after marriage; set calendar reminder for wedding + 30 days

general_rules.frequency: Every year, same time (e.g., January, birthday, anniversary)
general_rules.purpose: Catch changes in relationships, new assets, deceased beneficiaries

general_rules.reason: If primary predeceases you and no contingent listed, assets go to estate (probate)
general_rules.minimum: Name at least one contingent for every account

general_rules.exception: Small accounts ($10K or less) may be okay via UTMA, but trust still better

general_rules.requirement: Beneficiary designations should align with will and trust structure
general_rules.common_mistake: Will says one thing, beneficiaries say another—beneficiaries win

general_rules.reason: Spousal inherited IRA has unique tax benefits
general_rules.exception: If spouse has plenty of own resources, can name children/trust as primary

general_rules.reason: Forces probate, defeats purpose of beneficiary designation
general_rules.only_exception: Very rare situations where estate needs liquidity for debts/taxes

general_rules.definition: If beneficiary dies before you, their share goes to their children
general_rules.example: Name 'my children, per stirpes' so if child predeceases you, grandchildren receive that child's share

retirement_accounts.spouse_primary: Usually best for tax reasons (spousal inherited IRA benefits)
retirement_accounts.trust_for_minors: If spouse deceased/no spouse, use trust for minor children
retirement_accounts.charity_ok: Can name charity as contingent (or primary if no family)

life_insurance.flexibility: No tax advantages to specific beneficiaries (death benefits tax-free)
life_insurance.trust_common: Often best to name trust for children as primary
life_insurance.spouse_or_trust: Either spouse OR trust (or both as co-beneficiaries)

bank_accounts_pod.simple_transfers: Good for small accounts, simple distributions
bank_accounts_pod.multiple_beneficiaries: Can name multiple people to split equally
bank_accounts_pod.immediate: Transfers immediately upon death with death certificate

step_1.task: List ALL accounts with beneficiary designations

step_2.task: Document current beneficiaries for each account

red_flags: Minor children named directly (not via trust)

actions: Request beneficiary change forms from each account custodian
Create trust if needed (for minor children beneficiaries)
Keep copies with other estate planning documents

step_5.recommendation: Calendar event every January 15: 'Annual beneficiary designation review'
step_5.also_review_after: Marriage, divorce, births, deaths, new accounts

married_with_children.age_range: Any age, married with minor children

typical_approach.rationale: Tax benefits for spouse on retirement; trust ensures child protection

single_parent.age_range: Any age, sole parent with minor children

typical_approach.rationale: Ensure professional management for children's benefit

divorced_with_children.age_range: Any age, divorced, children from prior marriage

typical_approach.solution: Typically requires QTIP trust or separate trusts
typical_approach.strategy: Provide for current spouse, ensure own children ultimately receive

key_takeaways: Beneficiary designations TRUMP wills—they control distribution regardless of will provisions
For most people, largest assets (retirement accounts, life insurance) pass by beneficiary, not will
Never name minor children directly—always use trust as beneficiary
Always name contingent beneficiaries—without them, assets go to estate (probate)
Update beneficiaries immediately after divorce—ex-spouses often still receive assets years later
Never name 'my estate' as beneficiary—defeats purpose and forces probate
Review beneficiaries annually and after all major life events
In {{STATE_NAME}}, some states automatically revoke ex-spouse beneficiaries, but don't rely on this—update explicitly
